Introduction:
In 2022, 22 million children missed their first dose of the measles vaccine compared to 19 million who had missed the same vaccine in 2019 [ 1 ]. Besides the recent COVID-19 pandemic [ 2 ], notable factors contributing to delayed vaccination uptake included parental lack of information, difficult access to health facilities, lack of finance and parental support, and distrust in vaccines and vaccination programs [ 3 ]; health worker scarcity and inadequacies along the vaccine cold chain and vaccine supply affect vaccine coverage [ 3 ]; and, poor coverage rates for birth dose vaccines in the immediate postnatal period, with the pooled coverage rates for Bacillus Calmette-Guerin (BCG) being at 14.2% within 0–1 days following birth and a 1.3% pooled coverage rate for birth dose of hepatitis B vaccine [ 4 ]. A study in informal urban settlements in Nairobi, Kenya revealed a 67% full vaccination coverage by one year, a higher number of missed opportunities, and low coverage of routine childhood vaccination, primarily given at later ages [ 5 ]. In these settlements, 22% of fully immunized children received their vaccines out-of-sequence (receiving BCG, measles, pentavalent, and polio doses outside the recommended schedule) and 18% did not receive the pentavalent with polio vaccine, contrary to existing recommendations [ 5 ].

Untimely birth dose vaccine administration means the newborns remain unprotected from vaccine-preventable diseases in the period when they are most vulnerable to morbidity and mortality, requiring interventions to address this problem. Text message reminders might improve the timeliness of birth dose vaccine administration as they keep individuals aware of vaccination schedules. Text message reminders are known to improve the completeness and timeliness of childhood immunizations in a cluster randomized trial at four primary healthcare facilities in Nigeria [ 6 ]. A systematic review and meta-analysis of 131 studies found text message reminders increased antenatal care clinic attendance and timeliness of child immunization [ 7 ]. However, the current evidence comes from stable populations—populations without several of the additional barriers like low health service coverage and poor uptake of health services experienced by informal urban settlements. Therefore, there is uncertainty around the effectiveness of text message reminders in improving immunization uptake in an urban informal settlement as the populations are mobile. Mobile populations are at risk for untimely and incomplete vaccination as the majority are less familiar with health services, more likely to have insufficient resources to reach health facilities, and less likely to use the same health facility regularly among other plausible reasons. In-person reminders through lay community health workers (CHWs) are unlikely to reach most of the caregivers as they frequently change locations and are unavailable during routine work hours.

Text reminders might address parental forgetfulness and enhance communication regarding vaccination appointments and will reach mobile caregivers who are unlikely to be found at home. We leveraged the widespread use of mobile phones and text reminders as a low-cost intervention to nudge parents toward timely vaccinations, ultimately increasing immunization rates.

Accordingly, we evaluated the effectiveness of text message reminders in improving the timeliness of birth dose vaccine administration (oral polio vaccine [OPV] 0 and BCG given at birth or within 2 weeks of birth) among newborns in the Viwandani urban informal settlement in Nairobi County, Kenya.
Methods and materials:
### Study design and setting

We conducted an open-label, stepped-wedge cluster-randomized pilot trial between December 2019 and April 2020 in the Viwandani urban informal settlement in Nairobi County in Kenya [ 8 ]. Viwandani is included in the Nairobi Urban Health and Demographic Surveillance System site [ 8 ]. The rationale for the trial design was based on the potential benefits of the intervention in improving the uptake of birth dose vaccines so withholding it from certain participants would be unethical, unacceptable, logistical inefficient, and inequitable. The trial site has a total population of 49 000 people, an annual birth rate of 16 per 1000 population, an infant mortality rate of 34.7 deaths per 1000 live births, and timely vaccination coverage of 22% [ 5 ]. Viwandani is composed of a mobile population [ 9 , 10 ], served by private health facilities and two public health facilities that provide free routine immunization services although both are located outside the area [ 5 ] and characterized by poor uptake of and access to health services, especially vaccination [ 11 , 12 ]. For this study, we considered eight villages that were divided into three blocks, with the first and second blocks having three villages each and the third block having two villages. This trial was not registered as it was a pilot.

### Participants, recruitment, and procedure

The study enrolled pregnant women residing in Viwandani who were in their second or third trimester. The participants were eligible if they met the following criteria; a pregnant woman owned a mobile phone and had no plans to relocate from the study village within six months of enrollment, and were willing to be enrolled and followed until two months after giving birth. The exclusion criteria were: pregnant women who had documented complications of pregnancy as assessed by health workers, women who planned to vaccinate their baby outside the Viwandani clinics, those who experienced adverse pregnancy outcomes during follow-up such as abortion, stillbirth, or early neonatal death, or those diagnosed with multiple pregnancies. Participant recruitment was conducted by lay CHWs targeting all pregnant mothers in their second or third trimester in the eight villages in Viwandani until the required sample size of mother–baby pairs was reached.

Enrolment into the intervention group was conducted sequentially through a public lottery randomization approach, two months apart, starting with block one (three villages), then block two (three villages), and lastly block three (two villages). Village assignment to any of the three blocks was done at random. The names of the blocks (cluster) were written on a piece of paper, sealed in an opaque envelope, placed in an opaque box, and thoroughly mixed. A village representative randomly selected an opaque sealed envelope without replacement, opened it, and revealed the assignment block for the village to the public. The blocks were thereafter randomly assigned to the intervention initiation time through a simple randomization approach. Here, the three blocks were randomly assigned to the intervention time using a computer-generated table of random numbers. By default, it was difficult to blind the study participants, investigators, and data collectors to the intervention so the trial was open-label.

### Baseline covariates

Trained lay CHWs used electronic/digitized forms installed on their mobile phones to collect data on the participant's background information, and data on the last menstrual period were abstracted from the antenatal care booklets upon obtaining informed consent. Mothers without ANC cards were asked to provide the data of their last normal menstruation period and if they did not know, they stated how many months their pregnancy had lasted and this was used to estimate their date of last menstrual period. The baseline data included socio-demographic variables such as maternal age, maternal level of education, marital status, household wealth tertiles (lowest, middle, and highest), and village name. Additional variables included calendar month and randomization block. Data on household characteristics including socio-economic status and childhood vaccinations were extracted from the Nairobi Urban Health Demographic Survey Surveillance database and then merged with the data collected through the digital platform using a unique household identification number.

### Intervention vs. control periods

The intervention was text message reminders provided to all participants in a phased manner, with the transition from the control period to the intervention period being every two months. In general, the intervention involved an interaction between lay CHWs, pregnant women, and healthcare workers using a mobile phone application linked to a central registry. Two lay CHWs selected from each village were trained to register all pregnant women in their second or third trimester using a mobile phone. The lay CHWs captured demographic variables of the pregnant women including age of gestation, expected date of birth, preferred health facility for delivery, and the village of residence at registration, and relayed the data to a central database. This triggered automated reminder messages to pregnant women through their mobile phones, lay CHWs, family members, or a friend about when the women were expected to deliver.

At delivery, lay CHWs documented the date of delivery of the child and submitted the data to the central database. The participants received three standardized text message reminders notifying them to consider taking their babies for timely vaccination during the intervention period. The first text message reminder was sent upon registration, the second was sent two weeks before the expected delivery date, and the last was sent on the expected date of delivery. At the vaccination point, the child's vaccination status was updated by lay CHWs or health workers, and the data were again relayed to the central server. Both lay CHWs and the health facilities received bi-monthly reports about newborns who were due for vaccination to appropriately plan for vaccination services.

During the control period, participants received the standard maternal, newborn, and child health care package provided by health workers. Among others, the routine antenatal care package comprised four visits, enabling pregnant women to receive health education on nutrition, vaccination, birth preparedness, and complication readiness; testing for human immunodeficiency virus (HIV), syphilis, malaria, including blood grouping, and cross-matching; deworming using albendazole; access to ferrous sulfate and folic acid to prevent anemia; and malaria prophylaxis using sulphadoxine and pyrimethamine tablets. At birth, the babies are offered free vaccinations at the facility of delivery. Both private and public health facilities free vaccine from the government provided they are accredited as a vaccination center. In Viwandani several private facilities are not accredited to vaccinate babies but two public facilities and a few private ones offer vaccinations.

### Outcome

The primary outcome was the timely administration of birth dose vaccines, namely BCG and OPV. We created three binary indicators of whether a newborn received OPV 0, BCG, and OPV 0 and BCG.

Timely administration of birth dose vaccine was defined as receipt of the birth dose vaccines by the newborn at birth or within 2 weeks of delivery. The data were collected through cross-sectional surveys from a random sample of participants who received the text message intervention.

### Statistical methods

We hypothesized the intervention would improve the timely administration of birth dose vaccines from 22% under routine immunization [ 5 ] to 45%. Considering 0.04 intra-cluster correlation coefficient [ 13 ], a fixed cluster size of 12 children, and a 0.8 autocorrelation coefficient, a total of 479 mother–baby pairs were needed to achieve 80% statistical power at a 5% significance if the drop-out was 20% [ 14 ].

We summarized categorical data as frequencies and percentages, and numerical data as mean and standard deviation. We stratified baseline categorical data by the trial arm and performed Chi-squared tests to assess covariate balance. For numerical data, mean differences between the trial arms were tested using the Student’s t -test as the data were normally distributed. We applied the intention to treat analysis principle to compare the outcomes between the intervention and control periods. The trial outcome was binary but common (more than 10%) so the odds ratio would overestimate the intervention effect so the risk ratio is recommended [ 15 , 16 ]. We used a generalized linear mixed effects Poisson regression model with random intercepts, exchangeable correlation structure, and robust standard errors. Using random intercept accounted for between-cluster variability in the baseline outcome. We identified theoretically relevant baseline covariates a priori, including maternal age, maternal level of education, calendar time, and household wealth tertile. We adjusted for these covariates, clustering at the village level, and calendar time to control for temporal confounders.

We reported the findings as adjusted risk ratio (aRR) and 95% confidence interval (CI). Stata version 15 (StataCorp, College Station, TX, United States) was used for sample size computation and data analysis.
Results:
### Participant characteristics

Table 1 presents the distribution of participant characteristics between the intervention and control periods. The participants were similar regarding age categories ( P = .560), level of education ( P = .210), and wealth tertile ( P = .620) but different regarding marital status ( P = .02).

### Participant recruitment per block and time

Table 2 shows the mother–baby pairs recruited in each block and at each time point between the intervention and control periods. Overall, 491 mother–baby pairs who had received the intervention at various time points and also had complete data were included, which is slightly higher than the computed sample size. The rationale for over-recruitment in certain blocks was to compensate for the lower numbers of mother–baby pairs in the other blocks and to maintain the statistical power.

### Distribution of outcomes between intervention and control periods

Differences in the timeliness of birth dose vaccine administration were observed for all the vaccines, whether separately or combined ( Table 3 ). During the intervention period, the timeliness of OPV 0, BCG, and OPV 0 and BCG administration were 93%, 92.7%, and 92.1% compared to 80.9%, 81.6%, and 77.9% during the control period, respectively ( P < .001).

### Effect of the intervention on the timely administration of birth dose vaccines

Table 4 summarized the effectiveness of the intervention on the study outcomes. During the intervention period, the timeliness of OPV 0 administration (adjusted RR [aRR] 1.16, 95% CI: 1.00–1.35), BCG (aRR 1.14, 95% CI: 0.98–1.33), and OPV or BCG (aRR 1.19, 95% CI: 1.00–1.43) tended to improve compared to the control period, adjusting for other factors.
Discussion:
Our trial showed a trend toward improved timely administration of birth dose vaccines during the intervention period compared to the control period. The intervention effect was relatively larger for both OPV and BCG (19%) than separately for OPV (16%) and BCG (14%). The improvement in the timely administration of birth dose vaccines has public health and clinical significance as it contributes to reducing childhood-preventable diseases, including morbidity and mortality. Our findings are consistent with previous studies that show text message reminders improve health outcomes and health services utilization [ 6 , 7 ]. Prior randomized trials also revealed that text message reminders are effective in improving the utilization of recommended first-year vaccinations [ 17 ], primary care attendance [ 18 ], and antenatal and postnatal visits and all recommended first-year vaccinations [ 17 ], including HIV testing and maternal retention in care during the first 8 weeks following delivery in Kenya [ 19 ].

Timely initiation of vaccination in the first year of life is crucial as transplacental immunity declines rapidly over time thereby posing a significant risk for neonatal morbidity and mortality from vaccine-preventable diseases. Since vaccination coverage and timeliness are the two most important factors affecting population-level protection against preventable diseases, our findings illustrate that text message reminders could be an additional tool for improving vaccination coverage in an urban informal settlement in Kenya and similar settings.

The trend toward better timeliness in birth dose vaccines during the intervention period might be explained by the low intervention intensity as only three standardized text message reminders were sent to the participants and the shorter transition time between the intervention and control periods. A recent systematic review and meta-analysis of 88 randomized trials from 17 countries with nearly 1.7 million participants showed that incentives and increased access to immunization services are the most promising tools to improve vaccination uptake in low-income countries [ 20 ].

Therefore, our findings suggest text message reminders could be combined with incentives and/or approaches to increase access to vaccination services to improve the timeliness of birth dose vaccines. For example, text message reminders could be combined with improved routine immunization access, outreaches, or incentives. Future research should assess such intervention packages [ 20 ]. Lastly, the possibility of the John-Henry effect cannot be ignored—during the control period, the participants might have changed their behavior by working hard to compensate for not being offered the intervention hence impacting the intervention effect [ 21 ]. Interpretations of our findings should consider these issues, and the data should be considered preliminary for larger randomized trials.

Our trial has several strengths. The trial is among the first to demonstrate the use of text message reminders in improving the administration of birth dose vaccines in an urban informal settlement in Kenya and sub-Saharan Africa. We employed a rigorous trial design to demonstrate a cause–effect relationship. The pragmatic trial was conducted in a real-world setting as the usual service providers implemented the intervention. Therefore, scaling up the intervention would not pose a major challenge as contextual factors were not manipulated. However, there are limitations. First, we lack data on specific barriers and facilitators to intervention uptake. The data would have strengthened the findings including informing scalability. Second, the findings are limited to birth dose vaccines and might not apply to all childhood vaccines. Third, the findings are limited to a shorter intervention period so the long-term intervention effects remain unknown.

Fourth, the post-estimation intra-cluster correlation coefficient was very tiny, suggesting that the variation in outcomes within the clusters is relatively low compared to that between the individuals across the entire study population. This reduces the trial's statistical power in detecting the intervention effect when the clusters are taken into account, making it difficult to detect treatment effects at the cluster level. However, a stepped-wedge cluster-randomized trial was relevant for ethical and logistical reasons, including controlling for temporal/time trends or other external factors that might influence the outcome. Lastly, we do not have data on contamination so we could not estimate the per-protocol effects of the intervention.
Conclusion: In this pilot randomized trial, text message reminders improved the timely administration of birth dose vaccines among newborns in an informal urban settlement. These findings suggest that text message reminders might serve as an additional tool for improving the timeliness of administering vaccines and improving the performance of vaccination programs in an informal urban settlement.
Ethics approval: Ethical review and approval were from the Amref Institutional Review Board (Amref ESRC P538/2018). We obtained additional permits and approvals from the National Research Commission and participating health facilities. All participants gave written informed consent before involvement in the study.
